\title{A no-go theorem and a bounded exclusion of exceptional points in the
massive scalar spectrum of doubly rotating five-dimensional Myers--Perry black
holes}

% NOT FOR SUBMISSION until these four fields are supplied.
% revtex expands the author block eagerly, so plain text is used here rather
% than a formatting macro.
\author{AUTHOR NAME NOT ASSIGNED}
\email{corresponding.author@NOT-ASSIGNED}
\affiliation{AFFILIATION NOT ASSIGNED. ORCID NOT ASSIGNED.}

\date{\today}

\begin{abstract}
We ask whether the enhanced symmetry of the equal-spin surface organizes
defective (exceptional) degeneracies in the massive scalar quasinormal spectrum
of the asymptotically flat, doubly rotating five-dimensional Myers--Perry black
hole. Our first result is exact. Because $\partial_\phi$ and $\partial_\psi$
remain Killing for arbitrary rotation parameters, the quasinormal pencil admits
an invariant decomposition into azimuthal sectors $(m_1,m_2)$, and the Jordan
chains of such a decomposition are the union of the chains of its summands.
A coincidence of frequencies drawn from distinct sectors therefore cannot by
itself create defectiveness: any Jordan chain of length greater than one must
already occur within a single fixed sector. The equal-spin multiplets, whose
members carry distinct $(m_1,m_2)$, are accordingly protected from
\emph{hybridization} --- their frequencies may and do separate as parameters
vary, but they cannot coalesce into a shared defective block. A residual Klein
four-group acting on parameters \emph{and} sector labels renders diagonal
sectors $m_1=m_2$ exactly even in the spin asymmetry $\delta$; when the
associated discriminant curve crosses $\delta^2=0$ transversally, the physical
exceptional branches must occur in mirror pairs and terminate quadratically on
the equal-spin surface. Our second result is numerical and explicitly bounded.
Searching the one channel the theorem leaves open --- collisions between
distinct $(\ell,N)$ branches inside a fixed sector --- over an atlas of
$50\,558$ continued modes in seven sectors, we find no exceptional point within
the declared domain, where the minimum separation between tracked branches is
$0.5116$ in units of the inverse horizon scale. The ten tightest candidates are
classified as avoided crossings by argument-principle, monodromy and Puiseux
tests. We emphasize that this is an exclusion within a declared domain: higher
overtones, higher angular branches, and the quasiresonant regime --- where no
recurrence-free solver is applicable --- were not searched.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

%=========================================================================
\section{Introduction}\label{sec:intro}
%=========================================================================

Quasinormal modes are the resonances of a black hole and the observable content
of the ringdown~\cite{Kokkotas1999D46,Berti2009D47,Konoplya2011D48,%
Bertietal2025D50}. Because the governing operator is not self-adjoint, its
spectral theory admits structures with no Hermitian analogue, the sharpest being
the \emph{exceptional point} (EP): a parameter value at which eigenvalues
\emph{and} eigenvectors coalesce and the generator becomes
defective~\cite{KatoE71,Bergholtz2019E63,Ashida2020E64}. There the resolvent
acquires a second-order pole, the mode expansion ceases to be a basis, and the
time-domain response develops a secular
$t\,e^{-\ii\omega t}$~\cite{PanossoMacedoetal2025B30,Motohashi2024B24}.

Such structures are documented across black-hole perturbation theory: branching
in nearly extremal Kerr~\cite{Yangetal2012B18}, eigenvalue repulsions in
Kerr--Newman~\cite{Diasetal2021B19,Dias2022B20,Davey2023B21}, genuine
exceptional points for massive scalars on
Kerr~\cite{Cavalcante2024B22,Cavalcante2024B23,Cavalcante2025B29}, and resonant
excitation near such points~\cite{Oshita2025B25,Yang2025B26,Kubota2025B27,%
Caoetal2025B28,Wang2026B32}. Most directly relevant, continuous
\emph{exceptional lines} occur for massive scalars on Kerr--de Sitter and
Myers--Perry--de Sitter, where the near-Nariai limit permits a semi-analytic
treatment~\cite{Nakamoto2026A17,Daveyetal2022A13,Ponglertsakul2020A12}. In the
non-Hermitian literature exceptional sets are generically of codimension two,
and symmetry can lower the codimension of higher-order
points~\cite{Bergholtz2019E63,Mandal2021E65,Zhangetal2022E66}.

The five-dimensional Myers--Perry black
hole~\cite{Myers1986A01,Emparan2008A02} is a natural arena. The massive
Klein--Gordon equation separates for arbitrary
$a,b$~\cite{Murata2007A03,Wu2008A04}; the two-spin massive scalar spectrum has
been computed~\cite{Huang2025A16,Lietal2023A15,Lu2023A14}; and the isometry
group is enhanced at equal angular momenta,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:enhancement}
  \mathbb{R}\times U(1)\times U(1)\ \longrightarrow\
  \mathbb{R}\times SU(2)\times U(1),
\end{equation}
rendering the metric cohomogeneity-one~\cite{Murata2008A06} and producing exact
degeneracies. The natural expectation, and the standard mechanism in
non-Hermitian systems~\cite{Zhangetal2022E66,Mandal2021E65}, is that breaking
the symmetry unfolds those degeneracies into exceptional points.

We show that this expectation fails for an exact reason
(Sec.~\ref{sec:nogo}), classify the residual discrete symmetry and its
consequence for any exceptional locus (Sec.~\ref{sec:group}), and then search
the surviving channel numerically (Secs.~\ref{sec:numerics}--\ref{sec:results}).

\emph{Statement of claims.} We claim (i) an exact structural theorem: a
coincidence of frequencies from distinct azimuthal sectors cannot by itself
produce a Jordan chain; (ii) an exact symmetry classification, with a
conditional termination law for diagonal-sector exceptional loci; and (iii) a
\emph{bounded} numerical exclusion of exceptional points within an explicitly
declared parameter domain. Claim (iii) is not a statement about the system as a
whole: overtones $N>3$, angular branches beyond those listed, the region
$s>0.45$ or $\mu>1.8$, and the quasiresonant regime lie outside it, and we make
no claim there.

%=========================================================================
\section{The separated problem}\label{sec:setup}
%=========================================================================

In Boyer--Lindquist-like coordinates $(t,r,\theta,\phi,\psi)$ with
$\theta\in[0,\pi/2]$ the metric reads
\begin{align}\label{eq:metric}
  \dd s^2 =\ & -\dd t^2
    + \frac{M}{\Sigma}\Big(\dd t - a\sin^2\!\theta\,\dd\phi
      - b\cos^2\!\theta\,\dd\psi\Big)^{\!2} \nonumber\\
    &+ \frac{\Sigma}{\Delta}\,\dd r^2 + \Sigma\,\dd\theta^2 \nonumber\\
    &+ (r^2+a^2)\sin^2\!\theta\,\dd\phi^2
     + (r^2+b^2)\cos^2\!\theta\,\dd\psi^2 ,
\end{align}
with $\Sigma = r^2 + a^2\cos^2\!\theta + b^2\sin^2\!\theta$,
$\Pi = (r^2+a^2)(r^2+b^2)$ and $\Delta = (\Pi - Mr^2)/r^2$. Here $M$ is the
Myers--Perry mass parameter, of dimension $(\text{length})^2$, \emph{not} the
scalar mass $\mu$; we set $M=1$. With $z=r^2$ the horizon polynomial is
$P(z)=(z+a^2)(z+b^2)-Mz=(z-z_+)(z-z_-)$, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:zpm}
  z_+z_- = a^2b^2 ,\qquad z_++z_- = M-a^2-b^2 ,
\end{equation}
a horizon exists iff $\mathcal{E}\equiv M-(|a|+|b|)^2\ge0$, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:horizondata}
  \Omega_a = \frac{a}{z_++a^2},\quad
  \Omega_b = \frac{b}{z_++b^2},\quad
  \kappa = \frac{r_+(z_+-z_-)}{(z_++a^2)(z_++b^2)} .
\end{equation}
We use the adapted coordinates $s=(a+b)/2$, $\delta=(a-b)/2$, so $\delta=0$ is
the equal-spin surface, and we quote the inner horizon as the \emph{radius}
$r_-$, with $z_-=r_-^2$.

With $\Phi = e^{-\ii\omega t + \ii m_1\phi + \ii m_2\psi}R(r)S(\theta)$ the
equation $(\Box-\mu^2)\Phi=0$ separates. The angular equation is
\begin{align}\label{eq:angular}
  \frac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}&\frac{\dd}{\dd\theta}
  \left[\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\frac{\dd S}{\dd\theta}\right]
  + \Big[\Lambda + (\omega^2-\mu^2)\big(a^2\cos^2\!\theta \nonumber\\
  &+b^2\sin^2\!\theta\big)
    - \frac{m_1^2}{\sin^2\!\theta} - \frac{m_2^2}{\cos^2\!\theta}\Big]S = 0 ,
\end{align}
and the radial equation
\begin{align}\label{eq:radial}
  \frac{1}{r}\frac{\dd}{\dd r}&\!\left[r\Delta\frac{\dd R}{\dd r}\right]
  + \Big[\frac{W^2}{r^4\Delta} - \frac{G^2}{r^2} - (a^2+b^2)\omega^2 \nonumber\\
  &+ 2\omega(am_1+bm_2) - \mu^2r^2 - \Lambda\Big]R = 0 ,
\end{align}
with $W = \Pi\omega - m_1a(r^2+b^2) - m_2b(r^2+a^2)$ and
$G = ab\,\omega - am_2 - bm_1$. We re-derived
\eqref{eq:angular}--\eqref{eq:radial} symbolically from \eqref{eq:metric} in
exact rational arithmetic; the derivation is re-executed as an automated test.
$\Lambda$ is normalized by $\Lambda=\ell(\ell+2)$ at $a=b=0$.

Introducing the spheroidicity $c^2\equiv(\omega^2-\mu^2)(a^2-b^2)$ and using
$a^2-b^2=4s\delta$ gives the exact identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:c2exact}
  c^2 = 4\,s\,\delta\,(\omega^2-\mu^2),
\end{equation}
so the angular operator reduces to the round Laplacian on $S^3$ on \emph{both}
$\delta=0$ and $s=0$, where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Lambdaround}
  \Lambda = \ell(\ell+2),\qquad \ell = 2n+|m_1|+|m_2|,\ n\ge0 .
\end{equation}
Moreover, at $\delta=0$ the radial problem depends on $(m_1,m_2)$ only through
$m=m_1+m_2$.

The point $z=0$ is an \emph{ordinary} point of \eqref{eq:radial} whenever
$ab\ne0$, since the apparent $1/z$ terms cancel through $W(0)=abG$ and
$P(0)=a^2b^2$; the equation is of confluent Heun type with regular singular
points $z_\pm$ and an irregular point at infinity. The quasinormal boundary
conditions are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bcs}
  (z-z_+)^{-\ii\sigma_+},\quad
  \sigma_+=\frac{\omega-m_1\Omega_a-m_2\Omega_b}{2\kappa},\quad
  e^{\ii\Omega r}r^{-3/2},
\end{equation}
with $\Omega\equiv\sqrt{\omega^2-\mu^2}$. Because $D-3=2$ the radial potential
is even in $r$ and has no $1/r$ tail, so the exponent $-3/2$ is exact and there
is no Coulomb phase, unlike four-dimensional massive
Kerr~\cite{DetweilerD53,Dolan2007D55}. We write the resulting nonlinear
eigenvalue problem as a holomorphic operator pencil $T(\omega)u=0$, with
$\Lambda=\Lambda(\omega)$ recomputed at every evaluation and never frozen.

%=========================================================================
\section{The sector decomposition and the no-go theorem}\label{sec:nogo}
%=========================================================================

\subsection{An invariant sector decomposition}\label{sec:nogo:decomp}

No component of \eqref{eq:metric} depends on $\phi$ or $\psi$, so
$\partial_\phi$ and $\partial_\psi$ are Killing for \emph{arbitrary} $a,b$, and
the torus $T^2=S^1_\phi\times S^1_\psi$ acts by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:torusaction}
  (\mathcal{R}_{\alpha\beta}u)(t,r,\theta,\phi,\psi)
  = u(t,r,\theta,\phi-\alpha,\psi-\beta).
\end{equation}
Quasinormal eigenfunctions are not square integrable, so we avoid $L^2$ and work
from the group action, stating the hypotheses explicitly since they are what the
argument consumes.

\begin{proposition}[Invariant sector decomposition]\label{prop:decomp}
Let $X$ be a Banach space carrying the pencil $T(\omega)$, and suppose
\begin{itemize}
\item[(H1)] $\{\mathcal{R}_{\alpha\beta}\}$ is a uniformly bounded, strongly
continuous representation of $T^2$ on $X$;
\item[(H2)] $T(\omega)$ and its $\omega$-derivatives commute with every
$\mathcal{R}_{\alpha\beta}$, and the domain of $T(\omega)$ is
$\mathcal{R}$-invariant.
\end{itemize}
Then the isotypic projections
\begin{equation}\label{eq:projectors}
  \Pi_{m_1m_2} = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^2}\iint
  e^{-\ii(m_1\alpha+m_2\beta)}\,\mathcal{R}_{\alpha\beta}
  \,\dd\alpha\,\dd\beta
\end{equation}
are bounded, mutually orthogonal idempotents commuting with $T(\omega)$, and
they separate points:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:separating}
  \Pi_{m_1m_2}u = 0\ \ \forall\,(m_1,m_2)\ \Longrightarrow\ u=0 .
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The integral \eqref{eq:projectors} converges as a Bochner integral by (H1), and
$\|\Pi_{m_1m_2}\|\le\sup_{\alpha\beta}\|\mathcal{R}_{\alpha\beta}\|$.
Idempotence and mutual orthogonality follow from the group law and the
orthogonality of characters. Commutation with $T$ and its derivatives is (H2).
For \eqref{eq:separating}, let $K_N$ be the two-dimensional Fej\'er kernel, a
nonnegative approximate identity on $T^2$, and set
\begin{equation}
  \sigma_N u=\iint K_N(\alpha,\beta)\,\mathcal{R}_{\alpha\beta}u
  \,\dd\alpha\,\dd\beta ,
\end{equation}
which is a finite positive combination of the $\Pi_{m_1m_2}u$. Strong continuity
and the approximate-identity property give $\sigma_N u\to u$ in norm. If every
$\Pi_{m_1m_2}u$ vanishes then $\sigma_N u=0$ for all $N$, hence $u=0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}\label{rem:whatweuse}
We deliberately do \emph{not} assert that the Fourier series of $u$ converges,
nor that $X$ is an unconditional direct sum of isotypic subspaces; in a general
Banach representation neither is automatic, and neither is needed. Only
boundedness, commutation and the separating property \eqref{eq:separating} enter
the argument below, and all three follow from (H1)--(H2) by Fej\'er summation.
Hypotheses (H1)--(H2) hold in the standard realizations of the quasinormal
problem --- weighted spaces adapted to \eqref{eq:bcs}, and the hyperboloidal
realization~\cite{Jaramillo2020C36} --- because \eqref{eq:torusaction} relabels
two \emph{compact} coordinates, acts by isometries of \eqref{eq:metric}, touches
neither $r$ nor $\theta$, and leaves \eqref{eq:bcs} invariant, the horizon
exponent depending only on the sector's own labels. The decomposition is over
$(m_1,m_2)$ \emph{only} and does not use separation of variables in $\theta$;
see Sec.~\ref{sec:nogo:survives}.
\end{remark}

\subsection{Jordan structure}\label{sec:nogo:jordan}

A tuple $(v_0,\dots,v_{q-1})$ with $v_0\ne0$ is a Jordan chain of length $q$ for
$T$ at $\omega_*$ if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:jordanchain}
  \sum_{i=0}^{j}\frac{1}{i!}\,T^{(i)}(\omega_*)\,v_{j-i} = 0,
  \qquad j=0,\dots,q-1 .
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:directsum}
Under Proposition~\ref{prop:decomp}, every Jordan chain of $T$ at $\omega_*$
projects componentwise onto Jordan chains of the sector restrictions
$T_{m_1m_2}$, at least one of which is nontrivial and of the same length;
conversely a chain in one sector extends by zero. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:maxchain}
  \max_{\text{chains of }T}q
  \;=\;\max_{(m_1,m_2)}\ \max_{\text{chains of }T_{m_1m_2}}q .
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Apply $\Pi_{m_1m_2}$ to the $j$-th equation of \eqref{eq:jordanchain};
boundedness and commutation with every $T^{(i)}$ give the same relation for the
projected components, so $(\Pi_{m_1m_2}v_0,\dots,\Pi_{m_1m_2}v_{q-1})$ is a
chain in that sector. By \eqref{eq:separating}, $v_0\ne0$ forces
$\Pi_{m_1m_2}v_0\ne0$ for at least one sector, whose chain then has length $q$.
The converse is immediate, and \eqref{eq:maxchain} follows.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Cross-sector no-go]\label{thm:nogo}
A coincidence of quasinormal frequencies belonging to \emph{distinct} azimuthal
sectors cannot by itself create defectiveness. Any Jordan chain of length
greater than one at $\omega_*$ must already occur within a single fixed
$(m_1,m_2)$ sector.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Immediate from Lemma~\ref{lem:directsum}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The wording is chosen so as not to exclude the case in which two sectors share a
frequency while one of them independently contains an exceptional point. There
$T$ is defective, but the defectiveness belongs to the single sector and owes
nothing to the coincidence. The underlying algebra is
standard~\cite{KatoE71}; what is specific here is that
Proposition~\ref{prop:decomp} holds for \emph{all} $a,b$, so the conclusion is
not confined to the symmetric locus.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The equal-spin multiplets}\label{sec:nogo:multiplets}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:multiplet}
On the equal-spin surface the labels degenerate at fixed $(\ell,m)$ form
$\mathcal{M}_{\ell,m}=\{(m_1,m_2):m_1+m_2=m,\ |m_1|+|m_2|\le\ell,\
\ell-|m_1|-|m_2|\in2\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\}$, with $|\mathcal{M}_{\ell,m}|=\ell+1$
independently of $m$; summing over the $\ell+1$ admissible $m$ gives
$(\ell+1)^2$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For $m\ge0$ put $m_1=m-m_2$. The value $|m_1|+|m_2|=m$ is attained for
$m_2\in[0,m]$, that is $m+1$ pairs, while each value $m+2j$ with $j\ge1$ is
attained by exactly two pairs, $m_2=m+j$ and $m_2=-j$. The constraint admits
$j\le(\ell-m)/2$, whence
$|\mathcal{M}_{\ell,m}|=(m+1)+2\cdot\tfrac{\ell-m}{2}=\ell+1$. The case $m<0$
follows from the parity generator of Sec.~\ref{sec:group}. The admissible $m$
are $-\ell,-\ell+2,\dots,\ell$, so the level total is $(\ell+1)^2$, the
dimension of the $SO(4)$ scalar harmonic level.
\end{proof}

The members of $\mathcal{M}_{\ell,m}$ share the same radial problem at
$\delta=0$ and are exactly degenerate there, and they carry distinct
$(m_1,m_2)$, hence lie in distinct sectors. By Theorem~\ref{thm:nogo} that
coincidence cannot hybridize into a shared defective block at any $\delta$. It
is essential to state what this does \emph{not} say: the frequencies are free to
separate, and they do. Figure~\ref{fig:multiplet} shows the sectors $(1,1)$ and
$(2,0)$, which share $m=2$, meeting at $\delta=0$ and separating for
$\delta\ne0$. The protection is against hybridization, not against splitting.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig1_multiplet.pdf}
  \caption{Sectors $(1,1)$ and $(2,0)$ share $m=m_1+m_2=2$ and are exactly
  degenerate on the equal-spin surface, separating for $\delta\ne0$ ($\ell=2$,
  $N=0$, $s=0.20$, $\mu=0.6$). By Theorem~\ref{thm:nogo} the coincidence at
  $\delta=0$ cannot by itself be defective; the branches nevertheless split
  freely as $\delta$ varies.}
  \label{fig:multiplet}
\end{figure}

\subsection{What survives}\label{sec:nogo:survives}

Within a single sector, distinct angular branches $\ell$ are \emph{not} separate
summands: $\Lambda_j(\omega)$ depends on $\omega$, so they are branches of one
analytic family and Lemma~\ref{lem:directsum} does not apply to them. This is
why Proposition~\ref{prop:decomp} was established without invoking separation of
variables: a decomposition taken over $(m_1,m_2,\ell)$ would have proved too much
and would have been false. Collisions between distinct $(\ell,N)$ branches
inside a fixed sector are the surviving channel, and the rest of the paper
addresses them.

%=========================================================================
\section{Residual symmetry and a conditional termination law}\label{sec:group}
%=========================================================================

Two exact transformations act on (parameters, sector labels),
\begin{align}
  E:\ &(a,b,m_1,m_2)\mapsto(b,a,m_2,m_1), \label{eq:Egen}\\
  P:\ &(a,b,m_1,m_2)\mapsto(-a,-b,-m_1,-m_2), \label{eq:Pgen}
\end{align}
generating a Klein four-group $G=\{1,E,P,EP\}$, with
$E:(s,\delta)\mapsto(s,-\delta)$, $P:(s,\delta)\mapsto(-s,-\delta)$ and
$EP:(s,\delta)\mapsto(-s,\delta)$. No element acts on the parameters alone: each
also moves the sector. A parameter-space symmetry at fixed sector therefore
exists only in sectors stabilized by the corresponding element, as collected in
Table~\ref{tab:stabilizers}. In particular the convenient assertion that
exceptional sets come in quadruples under independent reflections $s\to-s$ and
$\delta\to-\delta$ holds only in the sector $(0,0)$.

\begin{table}[b]
\centering
\begin{ruledtabular}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
sector & stabilizer & induced symmetry \\
\colrule
$m_1=m_2$ & $E$ & $\omega(s,\delta)=\omega(s,-\delta)$ \\
$m_1=-m_2$ & $EP$ & $\omega(s,\delta)=\omega(-s,\delta)$ \\
$(0,0)$ & $G$ & even in $\delta$ and in $s$ \\
generic & $\{1\}$ & none \\
\end{tabular}
\end{ruledtabular}
\caption{Stabilizers and the induced parameter symmetries. All three nontrivial
cases are verified numerically below $10^{-12}$, with a negative control
confirming that a generic sector is not even in $\delta$ (Supplemental
Material).}
\label{tab:stabilizers}
\end{table}

In a diagonal sector every branch is even in $\delta$, hence --- granted
analyticity --- an analytic function of $t\equiv\delta^2$. The discriminant of
the local two-branch problem,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Ddef}
  D \equiv (\omega_+-\omega_-)^2 ,
\end{equation}
therefore depends on $\delta$ only through $t$, and an EP2 is $D=0$: two real
conditions, the familiar codimension two~\cite{Bergholtz2019E63}, defining a
curve in $(s,t,\mu)$. The physical space is the double cover
$\delta=\pm\sqrt{t}$, defined only for $t\ge0$.

\begin{proposition}[Mirror pairing and conditional termination]
\label{prop:termination}
Assume analyticity in the parameters and let $\Gamma$ be a component of
$\{D=0\}$ in $(s,t,\mu)$. The physical locus is invariant under $E$, so
exceptional branches occur in mirror pairs. If in addition $\Gamma$ meets $t=0$
\emph{transversally}, passing into $t<0$, then parametrizing $\Gamma$ by
arclength $\tau$ with $t\approx c\tau$, $c\ne0$, gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sqrtlaw}
  \delta = \pm\sqrt{c\,\tau} ,
\end{equation}
so the two mirror branches meet at $\delta=0$ and terminate, approaching the
equal-spin surface quadratically rather than crossing it.
\end{proposition}

The termination is conditional on transversality: a tangential crossing, or a
component remaining in $t>0$, is not excluded. This is the mechanism by which
the equal-spin symmetry constrains exceptional topology here --- not by
protecting a degeneracy, that channel being closed by Theorem~\ref{thm:nogo},
but by constraining the unfolding. It is the analogue of symmetry-constrained
exceptional structures in non-Hermitian lattice
models~\cite{Zhangetal2022E66,Mandal2021E65}, differing in that symmetry there
lowers the codimension of higher-order points, whereas here it acts on the
reality structure of the unfolding parameter. The prediction was recorded before
the numerical search and remains untested, no exceptional locus having been
found to exhibit it.

%=========================================================================
\section{Numerical formulation and admissible diagnostics}\label{sec:numerics}
%=========================================================================

\subsection{Solvers and benchmarks}\label{sec:num:solvers}

Solver~A is Leaver's continued fraction~\cite{Leaver1985D51,LeaverD52} applied
to the Gaussian-reduced Frobenius recurrence, of width $13$ for generic two-spin
parameters and $9$ in the static case. Solver~B uses the raw recurrence with a
Hill determinant and Wynn acceleration~\cite{Hatsuda2021D49} and is \emph{not}
independent of A. Solvers~C and~D are recurrence-free: an exterior
complex-scaled Chebyshev collocation and a multidomain near-horizon spectral
method. Solver~C's independence is enforced by a test that fails if any
recurrence routine is referenced. Any claim requires agreement between the two
families. Related methods are reviewed
in~\cite{Choetal2011D57,Lin2016D58,Linetal2017D59,Matyjasek2017D60,%
Fortuna2020D62}, with open implementations for Kerr in~\cite{Stein2019D61}.

Exterior complex scaling rotates the radial contour beyond a matching radius,
$r=r_m+\varsigma e^{\ii\vartheta}$, and requires
\begin{equation}\label{eq:anglecondition}
  \tan\vartheta > -\Imm\,\Omega/\Rem\,\Omega
\end{equation}
for the outgoing solution to decay along the contour; this returns in
Sec.~\ref{sec:results:limits}.

The five-dimensional Schwarzschild--Tangherlini fundamental scalar mode is
reproduced to all twelve published digits,
$\omega=0.533835574268-0.383375368513\,\ii$ at $r_+=1$, with absolute error
$5.0\times10^{-13}$ against~\cite{Matyjasek2021} and $2.2\times10^{-12}$ between
Solvers~A and~B. The exchange symmetry $(a,m_1)\leftrightarrow(b,m_2)$ holds to
$4.2\times10^{-15}$, and three solvers agree below $10^{-5}$ on ten benchmark
points. The atlas domain extends to $r_-=0.2287$, beyond the previously
validated $r_-\le0.19$; Solvers~A and~C agree to at most $2.06\times10^{-9}$ on
nine spanning points including the domain corners.

\subsection{What can and cannot serve as a bound}\label{sec:num:diagnostics}

Because the conclusion of Sec.~\ref{sec:results} is negative, the admissibility
of each diagnostic must be established rather than assumed. We record two that
are \emph{not} admissible, both being natural choices.

\emph{The derivative of the spectral condition.} A spectral condition $F$ is
determined only up to a nonvanishing holomorphic factor: Leaver's continued
fraction may be rescaled, or inverted at a different depth, without changing its
zeros. Under $F\mapsto gF$ one has $\tilde F'(\omega_1)=g(\omega_1)F'(\omega_1)$
at a simple root, so $|\dd F/\dd\omega|$ has no invariant meaning and cannot
bound the distance to an exceptional point.

\emph{The ratio of leading Taylor coefficients.} Expanding
$F=\sum_k a_k(\omega-\omega_1)^k$ about a simple root, $|a_1/a_2|$ approximates
the distance to a nearby second root. It fails as a bound for two independent
reasons. First, it is only \emph{asymptotically} insensitive to normalization:
under $F\mapsto gF$, writing $g=g_0+g_1(\omega-\omega_1)+\dots$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:a1a2distortion}
  \frac{\tilde a_1}{\tilde a_2}
  = \frac{a_1/a_2}{1+(g_1/g_0)\,(a_1/a_2)} ,
\end{equation}
so the distortion is $\Ord(|g'/g|\,d)$ with $d$ the separation. This is
measurable: for $g=Ae^{k\omega}$ the observed ratio follows $|1+kd|^{-1}$ to
five decimals, from $1.0003$ at $d=10^{-4}$ to $1.43$ at $d=0.1$
[Fig.~\ref{fig:calibration}(a)]. Second, and decisively, $|a_1/a_2|$ measures
the distance to the nearest zero \emph{or pole}. Leaver's continued fraction is
meromorphic, and contour integration about our tightest candidate returns
$\mathcal{N}-\mathcal{P}=0$ at every radius out to $0.20$: one zero and one pole
enclosed. The small values it returns are pole distances and carry no spectral
meaning. We therefore \emph{withdraw} this estimator as a bound and retain it
only as a local indicator.

What survives is admissible because it is built from eigenvalue differences of
independently verified modes: the pairwise separation between tracked branches,
each confirmed by an ODE residual of order $10^{-12}$ and by cross-solver
agreement; and the eigenvalue condition number
$\kappa=\|u\|\,\|v\|/|v^\dagger T'(\omega_*)u|$ computed from Solver~C's
collocation matrix, which is free of the continued fraction's poles. We note
also that the discriminant \eqref{eq:Ddef} is \emph{not} independent evidence,
being the square of the separation.

\subsection{Verification gate}\label{sec:num:gate}

For classifying individual candidates we use the argument principle, root
recovery from contour moments~\cite{KravanjaVanBarel2000}, monodromy, and the
Puiseux exponent, all calibrated on problems with known exceptional structure
--- $\lambda^2-t$, $\lambda^3-t$, $\lambda^2-(t^2+g^2)$, Jordan blocks --- and,
equally importantly, on negative controls in which the detector must not fire
[Fig.~\ref{fig:calibration}(b)]. Near a simple zero of $D$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:puiseux}
  \omega_\pm(t) = \omega_* + c_1t \pm c_{1/2}t^{1/2} + \Ord(t^{3/2}),
\end{equation}
so an EP2 exhibits $t^{1/2}$ splitting, a monodromy interchanging the branches
on one circuit and restoring them on two, and an enclosed zero count of two.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_calibration.pdf}
  \caption{(a) The coefficient ratio is only asymptotically insensitive to the
  normalization of the spectral condition: its distortion under
  $F\mapsto10^{7}e^{3\omega}F$ follows $|1+(g'/g)d|^{-1}$ exactly, reaching
  $43\%$ at $d=0.1$, whereas the enclosed zero count is unaffected. (b) The
  Puiseux exponent separates an EP2 ($t^{1/2}$) from an ordinary crossing
  ($t^{1}$) and from an avoided crossing, which saturates at a constant.}
  \label{fig:calibration}
\end{figure}

%=========================================================================
\section{Atlas, exclusion and limitations}\label{sec:results}
%=========================================================================

\subsection{The branch atlas}\label{sec:results:atlas}

Branches are identified by continuation history, never by sorting frequencies:
at an avoided crossing two branches exchange order in $\Rem\,\omega$ while
remaining distinct modes. Each step is seeded by quadratic extrapolation and
accepted only if the predictor miss $\varepsilon_{k+1}$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:misstest}
  \varepsilon_{k+1}\le\max\!\Big(4\,\mathrm{med}\{\varepsilon_1,..,\varepsilon_k\},\,
  0.02\max(|\omega_{k+1}|,1)\Big),
\end{equation}
the first argument being essential: the predictor miss is a local truncation
error and follows a smooth trend, so a branch jump appears as a sudden multiple
of the running median. A tolerance proportional to $|\omega|$ alone is a
constant, and admitted a jump in which the trend of $\Imm\,\omega$ reversed.

The atlas comprises $50\,558$ points over the seven independent sectors
$(0,0)$, $(1,1)$, $(-1,-1)$, $(1,0)$, $(2,0)$, $(2,1)$, $(2,2)$, with
$\ell\in\{\ell_{\min},\ell_{\min}+2,\ell_{\min}+4\}$ and $N=0,\dots,3$, over
\begin{equation}\label{eq:domain}
  s\le0.42,\ \ |\delta|\le0.20,\ \ \mu\le1.8,\ \
  r_-\le0.2287,\ \ \mathcal{E}\ge0.294 .
\end{equation}
The maximum continued-fraction residual is $3.6\times10^{-9}$; $118$
predictor-miss and $33$ non-convergence events are recorded rather than filled
in, and four branch-label collapses are excluded and counted. Two symmetry
predictions are recovered from independently computed frequencies as an
end-to-end check: the separations at $\pm\delta$ in diagonal sectors agree to
$\sim10^{-12}$, and sectors $(1,1)$ and $(2,0)$ agree at $\delta=0$ to
$9\times10^{-12}$.

\subsection{The bounded exclusion}\label{sec:results:bound}

Within the domain \eqref{eq:domain},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bound}
  \min_{\text{atlas}}|\omega_i-\omega_j| = 0.5116 ,
  \qquad \kappa_{\max}=8.73\times10^{3},
\end{equation}
the latter against $\kappa=18.3$ at an ordinary control mode. An EP2 requires
the separation to vanish and $\kappa$ to diverge; neither occurs. The minimum
separation is $\approx0.51$ where $|\omega|\approx2$--$4$, a relative separation
of order $15\%$, and it is attained on the \emph{boundary} of
\eqref{eq:domain}, at $s=0.42$, $\delta=-0.20$, $\mu=1.8$
(Fig.~\ref{fig:exclusion}).

The ten tightest candidates were put through the gate of
Sec.~\ref{sec:num:gate}. All ten are rejected with a common signature: two
distinct roots are present, but there is no coalescence, no monodromy
interchange, and no $t^{1/2}$ splitting. The classification is therefore
\emph{avoided crossing} --- the behaviour familiar from eigenvalue repulsion in
the Kerr--Newman family~\cite{Diasetal2021B19,Davey2023B21}, here without the
accompanying exceptional points. Consistently, the elevated but finite
$\kappa=8.73\times10^{3}$ is what one expects at a genuine avoided crossing.

\begin{figure}[t]
  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig3_exclusion.pdf}
  \caption{The bounded exclusion. (a) Level curves of the separation between the
  $N=2$ and $N=3$ branches at $\ell=4$ in sector $(1,1)$, on the equal-spin
  surface; the star marks the global minimum, which lies on the boundary of the
  searched domain (heavy axes). (b) Distribution of the tracked separation over
  the atlas. No claim is made outside the domain \eqref{eq:domain}.}
  \label{fig:exclusion}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Limitations}\label{sec:results:limits}

The exclusion is bounded, and we state the boundaries plainly. The minimum lies
on the edge of \eqref{eq:domain}; a targeted probe beyond it finds the
separation falling to $0.472$ at $s=0.45$ but rising again at $\mu=3.0$ and
$3.6$, so the trend does not extrapolate to zero --- yet no claim is made for
$s>0.45$ or $\mu>1.8$. Overtones $N>3$ and higher $\ell$ were not searched, and
highly damped overtones are known to be
delicate~\cite{Nollert1996C33,Miyachi2025C45}.

The quasiresonant regime was not searched. As $\mu$ grows, branches migrate
toward $\omega^2=\mu^2$ and the damping collapses --- we follow it through $8.6$
orders of magnitude, to $8.65\times10^{-10}$ --- and there $\Rem\,\Omega\to0$,
so by \eqref{eq:anglecondition} the minimum admissible scaling angle tends to
$90^\circ$ and no admissible contour exists. We measure $\vartheta_{\min}$ of
$89.92^\circ$ and $89.81^\circ$ where the recurrence-free solvers fail, against
$4.4^\circ$ at an ordinary near-extremal point where they succeed. This is a
limit of the formulation rather than a convergence failure, and it implies that
the difficulty in this range is controlled by $\mu$ and \emph{not} by proximity
to extremality: ordinary modes continue smoothly to $\mathcal{E}=0.0103$ with
residuals $\sim10^{-13}$. No independent confirmation being available there, the
standard of Sec.~\ref{sec:num:gate} cannot be met, and this is the one region of
the studied sectors in which an exceptional point could still be hiding.
Details are in the Supplemental Material.

Certification was attempted and is limited in
scope~\cite{MooreE73,TuckerE74,Breiding2020E69,Duff2024E70}: we obtain a
Krawczyk certificate for finite-dimensional systems and an Arb enclosure of the
angular eigenvalue of the truncated Jacobi matrix, validated by recovering
$\ell(\ell+2)$ at $c^2=0$. The radial problem is \emph{not} certified, its
recurrence coefficients being extracted by a discrete Fourier transform for
which we have no rigorous aliasing bound. No truncated-recurrence or continuum
certificate is claimed.

Finally, the numerical result is an exclusion over a declared domain, not a
theorem, and must not be conflated with Theorem~\ref{thm:nogo}, which is exact.

%=========================================================================
\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
%=========================================================================

We exclude exceptional points within the declared numerical domain; we do not
claim their absence from the system. Exceptional lines \emph{do} occur in the de
Sitter members of this family~\cite{Nakamoto2026A17}, and the present
$\Lambda=0$ result is a contrast between spacetimes rather than a
contradiction: the de Sitter mechanism relies on the cosmological horizon and
the P\"oschl--Teller reduction, neither of which has an asymptotically flat
analogue.

Within the asymptotically flat doubly rotating case the structure is sharply
organized. The most natural route to exceptional behaviour is closed exactly, by
the same symmetry that generates the candidate degeneracies. The surviving route
is numerically weak in the region searched: those branches repel with a
separation that never falls below half a unit. The parameter space has
\emph{exactly} the dimension at which codimension-two sets should be
generic~\cite{Bergholtz2019E63}, so their absence in this region is informative
rather than expected.

Two methodological points may outlive the application. First, neither the
derivative of a spectral condition nor the ratio of its leading Taylor
coefficients is an admissible bound on the distance to an exceptional point: the
former is not invariant under the renormalization freedom, and the latter
measures the distance to the nearest zero \emph{or pole} of a meromorphic
condition. Second, a small computed separation between two \emph{labels} is
evidence about the labels before it is evidence about the physics.

The natural next step is a hyperboloidal formulation, the only method that
remains applicable as $\Rem\,\Omega\to0$ and therefore the only route into the
quasiresonant regime~\cite{Jaramillo2020C36,PanossoMacedoetal2025B30}.
